ALTERWORLD ORIGINS · 1996—2002

The Adrock years.

Before browser games, cloud deployments, and GitHub Actions, there was a dial-up-era homepage, a home-built DOS environment, CGI message boards, and wrestling software written in Visual FoxPro. This is where Alterworld began.

8.4AlterWorld Wrestling release
6 yrsof surviving early work

Before “full-stack developer” was common language, this was already full-stack work: users, tools, data, community features, downloadable software, documentation, releases, and direct feedback loops.

Captured screens

INTERNET ARCHAEOLOGY

The progression

FROM DOS TO DYNAMIC WEB
1996

Alter/OS

A DOS-hosted, multi-user command environment with passwords, file management, an editor, calculator, terminal, announcements, online help, Windows launching, sound, ANSI screens, and a slot game. Documentation, installation, beta feedback, and version notes were part of the product.

1997

AlterHouse goes online

The first surviving homepage connected Alter/OS, BBS experiments, Ai2000, writing, community pages, original graphics, and MIDI. The web became both a distribution channel and a place to experiment in public.

1998—2000

From pages to applications

CGI list, post, and read modes powered message areas. Guest walls, a cookbook, personal databases, categorized lists, and AlterCam pointed toward a deeper interest in data-backed, participatory software.

2001

AlterWorld Software

Visual FoxPro became a playground for complete desktop products. Wrestling, bowling, fishing, and SecurePIC tested simulation, animation, data storage, security concepts, installers, and platform limits.

2002

AWW 8.4 ships

AlterWorld Wrestling grew from one predetermined match screen to real-time matches, tag teams, more than 40 wrestlers, an e-fed manager, and a franchise simulation with hiring, training, ticket prices, events, and advertising. Read the full AWW retrospective →

Things that shipped

PRODUCTS & EXPERIMENTS
1996

Alter/OS

An approachable command environment built on DOS, priced at $15 to cover advertising and disk mailing.

1999—2002

AlterWorld Wrestling

A long-running Visual FoxPro wrestling sim that evolved through years of releases and user feedback. Full story →

2000—2001

Bowling + Fishing

Two small games deliberately built to discover how far Visual FoxPro could be pushed.

2001

SecurePIC

A multi-user utility that encoded private pictures into a password-protected database.

1998—2000

Community tools

CGI message areas, posting flows, guest walls, link databases, and webcam-style pages.

2001

The Jay Show

A fictional series website with news, an about page, and seven surviving episode entries.

The through-line

The tools changed quickly, but the habits were already there: ship early, document the work, listen to testers, make the setup understandable, stretch the platform, and use every project as the laboratory for the next one.

Curiosity became working software. Working software became a product. Each product became the next experiment.
